title: Family
intro: Meeting and visiting your partner's family: forms of address, gifts, dinner, small talk and festivals.

scenes.title: Meeting your partner's parents: what to call them and what to say
scenes.description: How to address your partner's parents before marriage (叔叔/阿姨, or 伯父/伯母) and after the wedding (改口 to 爸/妈, usually at the wedding tea ceremony, with the 改口费 gift), short polite lines for a first visit, and what the hosts will say to you.

phrases.english: Uncle — what you call your partner's father (or any man of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: Before marriage a friend's or partner's parents are 叔叔 and 阿姨: in the official HSK 3 sample paper a man about to marry tells a friend '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来' (bring your parents — lit. uncle and auntie — along too). CC-CEDICT: 'form of address used by children for a male one generation older'; Xinhua: '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子' (general term for men of one's father's generation who are younger [than one's father]); for a man clearly older than your own father the matching title is 伯父/伯伯. Pair it with 您: HSK 3 sample '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？'. Children will in turn call you 叔叔 if you are a man of their parents' generation. Whether your partner's family expects 叔叔 or 伯父 is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Auntie — what you call your partner's mother (or any woman of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: The counterpart of 叔叔 (HSK 3 sample: '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来'). Xinhua: '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女：王～' (address for a woman of one's mother's generation and similar age, e.g. 王阿姨); CC-CEDICT: 'woman of similar age to one's parents (term of address used by child)'. HSK 5 sample: '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？' (a young man to a retired woman, with 您). 阿姨 is also how nannies and childcare workers are addressed (Xinhua sense ③; CC-CEDICT 'childcare worker; nursemaid'). Alternative pair: 伯父/伯母.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Xinhua marks only the kinship sense 'mother's sister' as dialectal (〈方〉); the title sense (王阿姨) has no regional label.

phrases.english: Hello, Auntie! (polite greeting with title)
phrases.usage: Title first, then the polite hello 您好 (CC-CEDICT: 'hello (polite)'; 您 = 'you (courteous, as opposed to informal 你)'). Adapted by one slot change from official HSK samples that put a title before 您好: '刘先生您好' (HSK 6) and '王教授您好，路上辛苦了。' (HSK 5). Swap the title for the person you greet (slot).
phrases.speaker: me

slots.meaning: the title of the person you greet

phrases.english: Sorry to bother you. / Sorry for the trouble.
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'sorry to interrupt you, but ... / sorry to have bothered you / sorry, I have to go'. In the HSK 4 sample a visitor who did not find the person ends with '好的，那我过一会儿再联系吧，打扰了，再见。'. So it fits when you interrupt someone and when you take your leave after imposing on them. CC-CEDICT also lists a slang sense (coined c. 2017, mostly online): said facetiously to end a conversation with someone insufferable — your tone makes the difference.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Thank you for your warm hospitality.
phrases.usage: A guest's thanks to the hosts. In the HSK 5 sample it is the guest's reply to the hosts' welcome at a dinner they give ('您好，王经理，欢迎来参加我们的宴会。' — '谢谢你们的热情招待。'); another HSK 5 sample has '谢谢你们的招待，…' at a banquet. 你们 = both of you / your family. CC-CEDICT 招待: 'to offer hospitality; to entertain (guests)'. Both samples are business dinners; the wording itself is not business-specific.

phrases.english: Your grandpa looks very young.
phrases.usage: Compliment from the YCT 4 sample ('你爷爷看上去很年轻。' — reply: '他身体不错，每天都坚持散步两个小时。'), said to your partner about a relative; swap the relative (slot). 看起来 works the same way (Tatoeba: '她看起来很年轻。'). To the person directly: 阿姨，您看起来真年轻！ (separate item). 你妈 is normal inside a sentence (Tatoeba: '你和你妈用上海话聊天的时候…'), but as a bare exclamation it is a curse (CC-CEDICT), so 你妈妈 sounds gentler when you speak of your partner's mother. CC-CEDICT 看上去: 'it would appear; it seems (that)'.
phrases.speaker: me

verification.notes: Wording independently confirmed by Tatoeba 2188409 '她看起来很年轻。' / 2188410 '他看起来很年轻。' (看起来 = 看上去 here). Correction in usage: the old text told learners always to say 你妈妈 because CC-CEDICT lists 你妈 as a vulgar interjection. That overstates it: 你妈 inside an ordinary sentence is everyday speech (Tatoeba 365616 '你和你妈用上海话聊天的时候，我只听得懂几个词…', said to a partner; 337981 '代我问候你妈妈。'); only the bare exclamation is a curse. The usage now says so and points to the new direct compliment item. Checker: OK. Previous values: usage = "Compliment from the YCT 4 sample ('你爷爷看上去很年轻。' — reply: '他身体不错，每天都坚持散步两个小时。'). Swap the relative (slot) to praise another family member; say 你妈妈 in full — CC-CEDICT lists 你妈 on its own as a vulgar interjection. CC-CEDICT 看上去: 'it would appear; it seems (that)'.".

phrases.english: Don't stand on ceremony. / No need to be so polite. / Don't mention it.
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'don't mention it / no formalities, please'. Hosts say it when you are being very polite; a guest can use it to wave away help or an offer: HSK 5 sample '不用，别客气，我的包不重，我自己来。' (refusing help with a bag); YCT 4 sample '谢谢王老师，您别客气，我刚喝了茶，不渴。' (declining a drink, to an elder, with 您). 不用客气 means the same (CC-CEDICT: 'you're welcome / don't mention it / no need to stand on ceremony').
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Uncle (respectful) — title for a man of your father's generation who is older than your own father
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'father's elder brother; term of respect for older man'. As a title it strictly suits a man older than your own father (Xinhua defines 叔叔 as the term for the younger ones). HSK 2025 lists 伯父/伯伯/伯母 at level 7-9 and 叔叔/阿姨 at level 3. Whether your partner's family prefers 伯父/伯母 or 叔叔/阿姨 at a first visit is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: As a title for a partner's father, 伯父 is understood everywhere. Don't carry over the northern kinship word 大爷 (= your own father's older brother in the north; see the paternal chart): said to an unrelated man, 大爷 is a title for an old man (现代汉语词典 大爷 ❷ '尊称年长的男子').

phrases.english: Mum — how you address your partner's mother once you are married
phrases.usage: After the wedding you 改口 (change how you address them): CC-CEDICT 改口 '…as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈'; 改口费 is given to the new daughter-in-law or son-in-law, so the switch concerns both. 妈 is the everyday short form; with 您 it stays respectful, as in the HSK 4 sample '妈，您的手机响了。'. Before the 改口, use 阿姨 (or 伯母). The switch usually happens at the wedding, during the tea ceremony (敬茶, also called 改口茶) when the parents hand over the 改口费; some families invite you to say 妈 earlier (for example once you are engaged or have registered the marriage) — wait for them to offer, and follow your partner's lead.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Hello, Uncle and Auntie! (greeting your partner's parents when you arrive)
phrases.usage: The usual greeting at the door: the title + 好, both parents at once — a ChinesePod lesson set at a girlfriend's parents' home opens with '叔叔阿姨好', and a maigoo.com article advises 叔叔阿姨 until the couple is engaged. Greeting each one separately (叔叔好！阿姨好！) works too — the same pattern as 大家好！ ('hello, everyone'). If the parents are older than your own parents, 伯父伯母好！ is the respectful variant. Then give your name (see 我叫…).

phrases.english: Sorry to put you to so much trouble. / Thank you for going to all this trouble.
phrases.usage: A guest's apology-cum-thanks when the hosts have gone out of their way — cooked a big meal, fetched you from the station, put you up for the night. Tatoeba: '给你添麻烦了，真的非常抱歉。' (I'm very sorry to have troubled you); 现代汉语词典 麻烦: '给你添了不少～' and the shorter '～您啦！' (= 麻烦您了！, Tatoeba 'Sorry to bother you!'). Use 您 for one parent; for both, 给你们添麻烦了 or 给叔叔阿姨添麻烦了 (slot).
phrases.speaker: me

slots.meaning: the person or people you have put to trouble

rules.rule: Speak to your partner's parents (and other elders) with 您, the courteous 'you', and put their title first: 叔叔，您…; 阿姨，您好. After marriage 您 stays respectful (妈，您…), but follow your partner's lead: many families, especially in the south, say 你 to their own parents.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 您 = 'you (courteous, as opposed to informal 你)'. The official HSK samples show younger speakers pairing titles with 您: '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？', '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？', '妈，您的手机响了。', '爸，您为什么要问我这么简单的问题？'. (Some samples show children using 你 with their own parents, e.g. the answer option '爸爸，你累了吧'; for an in-law, 您 is the courteous form.)
rules.regional_note: 您 is far more frequent in northern speech (Beijing above all); in the south many people say 你 even to elders in everyday talk, so 您 can sound a little formal there — but it is never wrong at a first meeting (anecdotal evidence: learner-forum reports).

rules.rule: Before marriage — and especially before you are engaged — call your partner's parents by kinship titles, as you would a friend's parents: 叔叔 (father) and 阿姨 (mother), greeting them with 叔叔阿姨好; or 伯父/伯母 if they are older than your own parents. Surname + title (王阿姨, 张叔叔) is the standard pattern for other older acquaintances, such as neighbours and family friends.
rules.why: HSK 3 sample: a man invites a friend's parents to his wedding as '叔叔、阿姨'. Xinhua: 阿姨 = '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女'; 叔叔 = '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子'. rules.rule: For men of your father's generation, 叔叔 fits those younger than your own father and 伯伯/伯父 those older. Within the family their wives are 婶婶 and 伯母; outside the family the usual title for a woman of your parents' generation is 阿姨 (伯母 goes with 伯父).
rules.why: Xinhua: 叔叔 = '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子'. CC-CEDICT: 伯 'father's elder brother … respectful form of address', 伯伯 'father's elder brother; uncle', 伯父 'term of respect for older man', 婶婶 'wife of father's younger brother', 伯母 'wife of father's elder brother'. relationship.js codes the same split: 'f,ob' (father's older brother) 伯父/伯伯, 'f,lb' (father's younger brother) 叔叔/叔父.

rules.rule: 改口: you switch to 爸/妈 (爸爸/妈妈) for your partner's parents at the wedding, usually during the tea ceremony (敬茶, also called 改口茶), and they give you 改口费. Before that use 叔叔/阿姨 (or 伯父/伯母), and don't start saying 爸/妈 on your own initiative: some parents invite it earlier (after the engagement or the marriage registration), and then you follow their lead.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT 改口: '…to change the way one addresses sb (as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈)'; 改口费: 'a gift of money given by parents on both sides after a wedding, to their new daughter-in-law or son-in-law'. 现代汉语词典/Xinhua 改口 ②: '改变称呼'. Web articles (search summaries): '敬茶又叫"改口茶"…当双方父母喝下新人们敬的茶后，还会给新人们改口费'; '若是两人还没有开始谈婚论嫁…就喊叔叔阿姨是最好的' (maigoo); parents who accept you may say you can call them 爸/媽 (Marie Claire Taiwan); following one's spouse in calling the in-laws 爸爸/媽媽 is still widespread (ETtoday, 2026).
rules.regional_note: Who gives 改口费, and how much, varies by region and family — in some places (reportedly especially North China) the bride's parents also give it to the groom. Ask your partner.

rules.rule: 公公/婆婆 (husband's parents) and 岳父/岳母 (wife's parents) name the relationship; once married you address them as 爸/妈. Before the wedding they are not yet your 公婆 or 岳父母.

The dictionary flags a parallel case explicitly: 小姨子 '(term not used to directly address her)'.

rules.rule: Kinship words double as polite titles for people who are not relatives: 叔叔/阿姨 for your parents' generation, surname + 爷爷 (张爷爷) for the grandparents' generation, 大哥/大姐 for people somewhat older than you, 大叔/大姨 for people about your parents' age.
rules.why: HSK 2025 syllabus: '姓氏+亲属称谓（张爷爷）'. Xinhua: 爷爷 sense 3 '对男性尊长的称呼'. CC-CEDICT: 大哥 'polite address for a man of about the same age as oneself', 大姐 'polite term of address for a girl or woman slightly older than the speaker', 大叔 'term used to address a man about the age of one's father', 大姨 'respectful term of address for a woman who is about the age of one's mother', 大娘 'aunt (polite address)'.
rules.regional_note: relationship.js readme: 大爷 can mean grandfather's elder brother or, in the north, father's elder brother. CC-CEDICT 大爷 dàye is also a 'term of respect for older man' — but dàyé (full second tone) means 'arrogant idler'.

scenes.title: First visit: arriving and giving gifts
scenes.description: Arriving at your partner's parents' home for the first time: greeting them, what to bring and what not to bring, handing over gifts modestly with both hands, the ritual refusal exchange, and being offered tea.

phrases.pinyin_as_source: shū•shu, āyí (XDHYCD headwords; the syllabus gives no pinyin)
phrases.english: Hello, Uncle! Hello, Auntie! (greeting your partner's father and mother)
phrases.usage: Greeting pattern "(称谓)+好！" (address term + 好) from the official function list, section 打招呼 (greeting). 叔叔 and 阿姨 are the dictionary-standard ways to address a man / a woman of your parents' generation who is not your relative; an HSK 3 sample dialogue uses 叔叔、阿姨 for (most likely) a friend's parents. Say it when you arrive, before handing over gifts. Slot: the address term; check with your partner which term the family expects (see the address-term rule below).
phrases.speaker: me

slots.meaning: address term (称谓) for the person you greet

phrases.regional_note: XDHYCD: strictly 叔叔 is for men younger than your own father and 伯伯/伯父 for men older than him; which term this family expects is a family/regional habit not researched here: ask your partner.

phrases.english: This is for you.
phrases.usage: Said while handing over a present. Built from the official pattern "(某礼物)+是送给你的" (gift + 是送给你的) in section 14. 馈赠 (gift-giving): the gift slot is 这 "this", and 您 (respectful "you") replaces 你 because you are speaking to your partner's parents (slot change). Same structure in an HSK 2 sample ("生日快乐！这是我送给你的。") and on Tatoeba ("这份礼物是送给你的。").

phrases.english: Just a small token (of my regard).
phrases.usage: A fixed modest formula listed in the official function list under 14. 馈赠 (gift-giving); say it as you hand over the gift, often after 这是送给您的. XDHYCD defines 心意 as "对人的情意" (kind feelings towards someone). The same list gives a much more formal "……，不成敬意，请笑纳" (it is not much, please accept it), and XDHYCD calls 笑纳 a 客套话 for asking someone to accept a gift. the attested forms are 一点儿心意 and 一点儿小意思.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: The 儿 is optional (XDHYCD writes 一点（儿））. Erhua is mainly a northern habit: with a south/central-China family you will mostly hear 一点心意, and in typed native dialogue 一点 without 儿 is the norm. Both are correct.

phrases.hanzi: 这是我的一点儿小意思。
phrases.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ de yīdiǎnr xiǎoyìsi.
phrases.english: This is just a little something from me.
phrases.usage: XDHYCD 小意思 sense ❶: "微薄的心意（款待宾客或赠送礼物时的客气话）" = a polite formula used when entertaining guests or giving presents; its example is "这是我的一点儿～，送给你做个纪念。" (the phrase here is the first clause). Note 小意思 also means "a trifle, no big deal" (sense ❷), so use it with the gift in hand. Also in the official gift-giving list as "一点儿小意思".
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 儿 optional, as above; in the south you will mostly hear 这是我的一点小意思. Careful: 小意思 on its own also means “no big deal” (e.g. as a reply to thanks).

phrases.literal: please accept this (measure word) small gift BA
phrases.english: Please accept this little gift.
phrases.usage: Use it to insist gently when the hosts protest that you should not have brought anything. 收下 is the verb for finally accepting a gift (XDHYCD 客气 example: “他客气了一番，把礼物收下了” — he made polite protests, then accepted the gift). Gift-etiquette guides say the hosts may decline two or three times before accepting, so keep offering warmly; a more colloquial push is 您就收下吧！ (see that item). Ask your partner how hard to insist in this family.

phrases.hanzi: 这是我从荷兰带来的特产，您尝尝吧。
phrases.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ cóng Hélán dàilái de tèchǎn, nín chángchang ba.
phrases.literal: this is I from Netherlands bring-come DE specialty, you (polite) taste-taste BA
phrases.english: This is a specialty I brought from the Netherlands, please try it.
phrases.usage: ADAPTED, not verbatim: the HSK 5 sample sentence is "这是我从海南带回来的特产，你尝尝吧。" (said by someone back from a trip to Hainan). Changes: place slot 海南 -> 荷兰; 你 -> 您; and 带回来 "brought back" -> 带来 "brought" (as in Tatoeba "从中国带来的龙井茶"), because XDHYCD defines 回来 as coming back to where one started — keep 带回来 only if you are returning home. XDHYCD: 特产 = a product special to a place or country, so it fits Dutch food specialties (尝尝 = have a taste; use it for food or drink only). Pinyin: CC-CEDICT has no entry 尝尝; the second syllable of a reduplicated one-syllable verb is neutral, as in CC-CEDICT 看看 kànkan.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.hanzi: 来就来嘛，还带什么东西！
phrases.pinyin: Lái jiù lái ma, hái dài shénme dōngxi!
phrases.pinyin_as_source: checker (CC-CEDICT citation tones: 嘛 ma5, 东西 dong1 xi5); the sources give no pinyin
phrases.literal: come just come MA, still bring what things!
phrases.english: You shouldn't have brought anything — just coming is enough!
phrases.usage: The ritual protest you will most likely hear when you hand over a gift. It means “having you here is what matters” (China News Service: 潜台词是“你人来了就好，不用送这送那的”) and is not a real refusal: keep offering (一点心意，您就收下吧！) and the gift will be accepted. A teaching page models the whole exchange: 一点小意思，你别嫌弃 — 哎呀，你太客气了，来就来嘛，还带什么东西！ Similar lines you may hear: 还拿东西干啥？ / 下次来可别买了.
phrases.speaker: them
phrases.regional_note: You may also hear 来就来呗 (呗 bei, another colloquial particle) with the same meaning.

phrases.hanzi: 你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收。
phrases.pinyin: Nǐ de xīnyì wǒ lǐng le, dàn lǐwù wúlùnrúhé bù néng shōu.
phrases.literal: your heart-intention I receive-LE, but gift in-any-case cannot accept
phrases.english: I appreciate the thought, but I really can't accept the gift.
phrases.usage: A firm, formal refusal, not the ritual protest: the official function list files it under 47. 拒绝 (declining), next to 这种礼物绝对不能收 (this kind of gift absolutely cannot be accepted), and 无论如何 means “in any case”. Dictionary variants: 我领这个情，但东西不能收 (XDHYCD 领情) and 您的美意，我心领了 (XDHYCD 心领: polite formula for declining a gift or a meal). It is what someone says who really must not accept (a teacher, an official) or when a gift is too expensive. On a family visit the protest you will usually hear is lighter: 来就来嘛，还带什么东西！ or 你太客气了！ (see those items). If you do hear this formula, do not keep pushing; ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: them

rules.rule: When you hand over a gift, your hosts will usually protest first (客气): 来就来嘛，还带什么东西！ (“just coming is enough — why bring anything?”), 你太客气了！, 下次别买了 (“don't buy anything next time”). This is a ritual: the real meaning is “having you here is what matters”, and a guest is still expected to bring something. Hosts may decline two or three times; keep offering warmly (一点心意 / 一点小意思, 您就收下吧！) until they accept. Fixed formulas such as 你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收 or 您的美意，我心领了 are different: they announce a real refusal.
rules.why: China News Service (2022) explains that 来就来呗 really means 你人来了就好，不用送这送那的; a teaching page models the exchange 一点小意思，你别嫌弃 — 哎呀，你太客气了，来就来嘛，还带什么东西！ and describes the first refusal as an opening move; a NetEase article lists 还拿东西干啥？ and 下次来可别买了 as host formulas not to take literally; a Shanghai etiquette wiki says the recipient may refuse 2 or 3 times while the giver insists (all seen as WebSearch summaries). The official 2002 function list files 你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收 under 47. 拒绝 (declining), next to 这种礼物绝对不能收; XDHYCD 客气❷: 他客气了一番，把礼物收下了.

verification.notes: Corrected: the old rule listed the firm refusal formulas as if they were the ordinary host protest, and said how many times to insist was unknown. Now the ritual protest lines come from current sources (Chinanews 2022, elon.io, NetEase, Shanghai wiki) and the firm formulas are labelled as real refusals (2002 list context, re-read from the page image). Previous values — rule: "When you hand over a gift, your hosts may first protest politely (客气) before accepting it. Fixed formulas for declining gifts exist (你的心意我领了，但礼物无论如何不能收 / 我领这个情，但东西不能收 / 您的美意，我心领了), and a dictionary example describes the whole sequence: 他客气了一番，把礼物收下了 \"he made polite protests, then accepted the gift\". Present the gift modestly (一点儿心意 / 一点儿小意思) and ask them to accept it (请收下这份小礼物吧)."; why: "Modesty on both sides is built into the standard gift vocabulary: the official function list has separate entries for giving (馈赠), accepting (接受) and declining (拒绝) gifts, and XDHYCD labels 心领 and 笑纳 as 客套话 (polite formulas). How many times to insist, and when a refusal is real, is not stated in these sources.".

rules.rule: On a first visit the elders may give YOU a present: a 见面礼 (jiànmiànlǐ) is "a gift given at a first meeting, mostly by the older person to the younger one" (XDHYCD). Thank them with 您 (谢谢您的礼物). A 红包 is money wrapped in red paper, used as a gift or reward (XDHYCD); these sources do not say whether a first-visit 见面礼 is usually money or an object.
rules.why: Dictionary definitions of 见面礼 and 红包.

rules.rule: Address your partner's parents with a title. The dictionary-standard titles for unrelated people of your parents' generation are 叔叔 (a man; strictly one younger than your own father) or 伯伯/伯父 (a man older than your father), and 阿姨 (a woman). Use 您 when you speak to them.
rules.why: XDHYCD defines 叔叔❷, 伯父❷ and 阿姨❷ as forms of address for non-relatives of the parents' generation; 您 is "你 (含敬意)", the respectful you.
rules.regional_note: In south and central China the maternal grandparents are usually 外婆/外公; 姥姥/姥爷 are the northern terms (the kinship library relationship.js lists 外婆/外公 first as the general forms and gives 姥姥/姥爷 in its 北方 locale). XDHYCD labels 外婆/外公 〈方〉 (dialectal), but in the south they are the everyday words. 您 is used much more in the north than in the south, but 您 to your partner's parents is polite everywhere. Titles can change after a wedding (改口, XDHYCD: 改变称呼, e.g. from 姐姐 to 嫂子): ask your partner what this family expects.

rules.rule: Typical gifts for a first visit to your partner's parents: fruit, tea, nutrition or health products (营养品, 补品 — choose them after asking about the parents' health), milk, and specialties from home (特产 — Dutch specialties fit well). Alcohol or cigarettes only if the father actually drinks or smokes, and then his usual brand. Bring something for both parents, not just for the father; even numbers are preferred (买双不买单); keep the value in line with the family's means. How many gifts are expected differs by region and family, so agree on it with your partner beforehand.
rules.why: one case shows a girlfriend's family asking for 18 items while the author thought six or eight were enough. XDHYCD: 补品 = 滋补身体的食品或药品; 特产 = a product special to a place or country.
rules.regional_note: Customs (number of gifts, money gifts, local specialties) vary strongly by region and family; ask your partner what their family expects.

rules.rule: Avoid these gifts because of how their names sound or what they stand for: a clock (送钟 sòng zhōng sounds like 送终 sòngzhōng, attending a dying elder or arranging their funeral — the classic taboo; sources disagree about watches, so avoid them for elders too); pears (梨 lí sounds like 离 lí “to part”) and umbrellas (伞 sǎn sounds like 散 sàn “to break up”), especially for a couple; shoes (鞋 xié sounds like 邪 xié “evil”); a green hat (戴绿帽子 means one's wife or partner is unfaithful); knives or scissors (cutting the relationship); white or black wrapping (colours of mourning — red and gold are festive); anything in fours (四 sì sounds like 死 sǐ “death”). Pairs and even numbers are preferred (“good things come in pairs”).
rules.why: English-language features in mainland media list the same taboos: People's Daily Online “Culture Insider: Taboos in gift-giving” (2015), China Daily “The art of giving to Chinese” (2015) and “Beware green hat gifts” (2008), The Beijinger (2020), and a Chinese Language Institute reader (seen as WebSearch summaries). The sound links are dictionary facts: XDHYCD 送终 = 长辈亲属临终时在身旁照料，也指安排长辈亲属的丧事; 戴绿帽子 = 称人妻子有外遇; 离 = 分离; 散 sàn = 由聚集而分离; 白事 = 丧事.
rules.regional_note: The sources date from 2008-2020; a Global Times story mentions a Chinese recipient who was happy with a clock, so younger urban people may be relaxed about some of these. For a first visit to elders, play safe.

sources.publisher: People's Daily Online
sources.evidence: WebSearch result summary (the page itself could not be fetched; direct fetches are blocked): one of the mainland-media pages returned for gift taboos (with chinaculture.org's copy). Summary lines: giving a clock is traditionally taboo because 'giving a clock' sounds like attending a dying person / a funeral; it is inappropriate to give lovers umbrellas and pears, which sound like separation; shoes (xie) sound like 'evil'; don't give a green hat, especially to a man ('wearing a green hat' means his wife is cheating); do not give knives or scissors, which symbolise cutting off a relationship; good things come in pairs, so pair gifts if possible; four sounds like 'death'; white and black should be avoided for wrapping, red and gold are preferred. The summary did not say which of the returned pages carries each line.

checked_sources.title: Culture Insider: Taboos in gift-giving
checked_sources.publisher: People's Daily Online
checked_sources.evidence: WebSearch result summary (the page itself could not be fetched; direct fetches are blocked): one of the mainland-media pages returned for gift taboos (with chinaculture.org's copy). Summary lines: giving a clock is traditionally taboo because 'giving a clock' sounds like attending a dying person / a funeral; it is inappropriate to give lovers umbrellas and pears, which sound like separation; shoes (xie) sound like 'evil'; don't give a green hat, especially to a man ('wearing a green hat' means his wife is cheating); do not give knives or scissors, which symbolise cutting off a relationship; good things come in pairs, so pair gifts if possible; four sounds like 'death'; white and black should be avoided for wrapping, red and gold are preferred. The summary did not say which of the returned pages carries each line.

rules.rule: Hand the gift over with both hands, and receive anything you are given with both hands. Do not expect it to be opened in front of you: traditionally a gift is put aside and opened after the guest has left, so that nobody loses face if it is not right — unless the giver insists or the people are already close. Chinese people who know Western customs may expect you to open a gift they give you straight away; either way is fine.
rules.why: Whether younger Chinese now usually open gifts on the spot is not documented in what was found.

scenes.title: Family dinner: eating, toasting, thanking
scenes.description: Seating and starting the meal, praising the food, hosts serving you food and refusing more politely, chopstick manners and serving chopsticks, toasting elders and drinking less (or not at all), the bill, thanking the hosts and leaving.

phrases.english: After you.
phrases.usage: Polite “after you” to an elder, e.g. when sitting down or before taking the first food. Tatoeba has “你先请！” (“After you!”); 您 replaces 你 for an elder (slot change). At a family meal you should not start until the most senior person has picked up their chopsticks (The Paper: 餐桌上辈分最高的人动筷之后，其他人才能动筷), so this line fits when the elders hesitate (see the seating rule).
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Cheers!
phrases.usage: The toast word. Literally “drain the cup”: XDHYCD 喝干杯中的酒, used to urge others to drink or to celebrate. So someone who says 干杯 to you may expect an empty glass. To drink less politely, see 我干了，您随意 (you empty yours, they drink as they like) and, if you do not drink alcohol, 我以茶代酒，敬您一杯.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: I wish you good health and a long life!
phrases.usage: A wish for an elderly person; listed word for word in the official list of wishes (祝愿: “祝你/你们/您 + 全家幸福！万事如意！…健康长寿！…”). 长寿 is said of old people (XDHYCD 长寿: 寿命长, example 长寿老人; 祝寿 = congratulating an old person on their birthday), so use it for grandparents; for your partner's parents 祝您身体健康！ or 祝您全家幸福！ / 祝您万事如意！ (same list) is the safer choice (slot: the wish).
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: I don't drink. / I can't drink alcohol.
phrases.usage: Declining alcohol (Tatoeba). If you are driving, the slogan "喝酒不开车，开车不喝酒" (if you drink, don't drive; if you drive, don't drink; Tatoeba) gives your reason. XDHYCD 酒量 ("how much one can drink") has the example "他酒量不行，喝一口就脸红" (he can't hold his drink, one sip and he goes red); with 我 it describes yourself (adapted). Hosts may urge you to drink (see the 劝酒 rule).

phrases.hanzi: 我今天开车来的，不能喝酒。
phrases.pinyin: Wǒ jīntiān kāichē lái de, bù néng hē jiǔ.
phrases.literal: I today drive-car come DE, cannot drink alcohol
phrases.english: I drove here today, so I can't drink.
phrases.usage: A standard reason for not drinking; then offer to toast with tea (我以茶代酒，敬您一杯). Wording from a learner dialogue (“我今天开车来的，不能喝酒。我以茶代酒，祝小王生日快乐！”); 我开车来的 “I came by car” is common in native-written dialogue (RiSAWOZ), and Tatoeba has the slogan 喝酒不开车，开车不喝酒. The 的 ending is the 是……的 pattern with 是 left out, stressing how you came.

phrases.usage: Offering to pay, e.g. when you take the family to a restaurant (Tatoeba; also "我来付钱。" "I'll pay"). phrases.hanzi: 什么钱不钱的，你这话说的太客气了。
phrases.pinyin: Shénme qián bù qián de, nǐ zhè huà shuō de tài kèqi le.
phrases.literal: what money not money DE, you this talk say DE too polite LE
phrases.english: Money? Don't talk like that, you're being far too polite.
phrases.usage: What you may hear if you offer to pay or mention money: example sentence of grammar point 355 "什么X不X（的）" (dismissing something the other person raised) in the 2021 standard. The standard prints 说的 here (说得 is the usual written form for this complement).
phrases.speaker: them

phrases.english: Please don't see me out.
phrases.usage: Guest to host who walks you to the door or beyond (official list: "[客人]：别送了/您留步"). XDHYCD 留步 is the more formal 客套话 for the same thing ("used by a guest asking the host not to see them out"): 您留步. An HSK 5 dialogue shows the host insisting anyway: guest "不用送了，赶紧回去吧，家里还有别的客人呢。" — host "没关系，已经出来了，就送到公交站吧。"

rules.rule: Chopstick manners: while talking, do not wave your chopsticks around; do not tap bowls, plates or the table with them; never point at people with them; when you put them down during the meal, lay them on the table or on the edge of your plate and never stick them (upright) into the rice bowl; avoid making noise with them.
rules.why: Stated in an official HSK 5 reading passage: “筷子……在使用上也有很多讲究。用餐过程中，如果说话，不要将筷子随便晃动，也不要用筷子敲打碗、盘子以及桌面，更不能用筷子指点他人，暂时离开时，要把筷子轻轻放在桌子上或餐盘边，不能插在饭碗里，而且尽量不要发出响声。” (the keyed answer is “说话时敲筷子不礼貌”). For serving chopsticks (公筷) and hosts putting food in your bowl (夹菜), see the separate rule.

rules.rule: When you clink glasses with an elder (or anyone senior to you), hold your glass so that its rim is lower than theirs; hold it in your right hand and support the base with your left (敬酒时杯子放低).
rules.why: An official BCT (B) sample keys “敬酒时杯子放低” (keep your glass low when toasting) as the right answer to listening question 41 (the audio text is not printed).

rules.rule: 干杯 literally means "drain the cup": it is used to urge others to drink or to celebrate, so a 干杯 aimed at you can mean that you are expected to empty your glass.

rules.rule: Hosts may urge you, repeatedly, to drink (劝酒) and to eat more. Decline with a short reason (我不会喝酒 / 开车不喝酒; 不了，我真的饱了) rather than a bare no.
rules.why: XDHYCD defines 劝酒 as "（酒席上）劝人喝酒" with the example "主人举杯频频劝酒" (the host raised his glass and kept urging people to drink), and 海量 ❷ has the urging line "您是～，不妨多喝几杯" (you can hold your drink, have a few more). Food urging appears in the YCT dialogue "别客气，再吃几个饺子吧 — 不了，我真的饱了". Giving a reason is advice drawn from the sample replies, not a stated rule.

rules.rule: Let the host seat you. The seat facing the door (the entrance) is the seat of honour (上座); at a family meal it normally goes to the most senior person or to whoever the host wants to honour, so do not take it yourself unless you are pressed to. Let the elders sit down first, and do not start eating until the most senior person at the table has picked up their chopsticks (you can invite them: 您先请).
rules.why: China Daily's table-etiquette guide (2024): “The seat facing the entrance is the most important and is usually reserved for the host or the guest of honor”; other guides say the guest of honour sits facing the door, in the 上座. The Paper (澎湃新闻) states the 长幼原则: 应当让年长的长辈首先就坐，然后年轻人再就坐, and 餐桌上辈分最高的人动筷之后，其他人才能动筷 (all seen as WebSearch summaries). XDHYCD: 上座 = the most honoured seat when seats are ranked; 让座❷ = the host inviting the guests to sit. The BCT sample keys 可随意就座 (sit anywhere) as not the right answer.
rules.regional_note: Guides differ on details (host vs. guest of honour in the seat facing the door), and families differ: follow the host's arrangement.

rules.rule: Leaving has a fixed exchange: the host sees you out and says 您慢走 / 您走好; you ask them not to come further (别送了 / 您留步), and they may still walk you to the bus stop.
rules.why: Official function list, section 告别: "[主人]：不远送了 [主人]：您慢走/您走好 [客人]：别送了/您留步"; XDHYCD 留步 is a 客套话 used when the host sees the guest off; HSK 5 dialogue in which the host insists on walking the guest to the bus stop.

rules.rule: Hosts may put food into your bowl or onto your plate (夹菜) to look after you: accept some and thank them; if it becomes too much, 不用不用，我自己来 or 够了，谢谢您！我吃饱了. Since 2020 many Chinese cities have promoted serving chopsticks and spoons (公筷公勺), and restaurants were asked to provide them; at home many families still take food from shared dishes with their own chopsticks, and some feel that serving chopsticks between family members are 见外 (treating each other as outsiders). If serving chopsticks are on the table, use them to take food from shared dishes and to serve others.
rules.why: XDHYCD 布菜 = 把菜肴分给座上的客人 (the host serving dishes to the seated guests); YCT/HSK dialogues show hosts urging food (别客气，再吃几个饺子吧; 再来点儿米饭吧，你吃得太少了). 公筷: Beijing News (2020) reports local regulations and proposals across China calling for 公筷公勺; a People's Daily group paper (2020) tells of a family switching to them; a health-news article names the resistance (“用公筷公勺就是见外”, “一家人吃饭还用公勺公筷太麻烦”) and a Shanghai survey with 92% approval (attitude, not use); an overseas Chinese paper notes serving chopsticks come out when guests visit (all seen as WebSearch summaries). CC-CEDICT 公筷 = serving chopsticks.
rules.regional_note: Practice varies by family; watch what your partner's family does.

rules.rule: You do not have to drain every glass. If you drink alcohol, you can empty your glass when you toast an elder and say 我干了，您随意 (“I'll finish mine, you drink as you like”). If you do not drink, give a reason (我今天开车来的，不能喝酒 — driving is a standard reason) and toast with tea or juice: 我以茶代酒，敬您一杯. Avoid 我就喝一点 (“just a little”), which invites endless top-ups, and do not say 我干了，您随意 while drinking tea.
rules.why: 我酒量不好 / 我开车 are the usual reasons and 以茶代酒 is an accepted alternative; one commenter warns about 我就喝一点 and about combining 以茶代酒 with 我干了你随意. XDHYCD 干杯 = 喝干杯中的酒; 随意 = 任凭自己的意思.
rules.regional_note: Drinking culture (how hard hosts press, 劝酒) varies by region and family; not researched here.

scenes.title: Small talk with elders and answering compliments
scenes.description: Greetings (including 吃了吗 and how to answer it), asking after an elder's health, the questions you will be asked (job, age, salary, wedding plans) with soft deflections, praising the weather and the place, and modest replies to compliments on your Chinese — including today's everyday forms (谢谢，我还在学习 / 没有没有).

phrases.english: Good morning! (to an elder)
phrases.usage: Morning greeting with the respectful 您, e.g. when you see your partner's parents in the morning during a stay. Listed in the official greeting list; XDHYCD uses "老师，您早！" as its example for 您. Neutral alternative: 早上好！
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 您早 is a typically northern (Beijing) greeting, and 您 is used less in the south; with a south/central-China family the neutral 早上好！ (or just 早！) may sound more natural.

phrases.english: Have you eaten? (a greeting)
phrases.usage: A greeting, not an invitation: the official list files it under 打招呼 (greeting), marked “[吃饭前后]” (around mealtimes) and “以下多用于中国人之间” (mostly used between Chinese people). The same list notes the habit of greeting by asking about what the other person is evidently doing (上课去呀？ / 去哪儿了？ / 回来啦！). Today you hear it mostly from older people and between neighbours or acquaintances; many younger urban people just say 你好 or “hi”. Answer briefly and return it: 吃了，您呢？ (or 我吃过了。 / 我还没吃。).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: How have you been keeping lately? (How is your health?)
phrases.usage: Asking an elder about their health: official 问候 list “你近来身体怎么样？ ——还好/马马虎虎吧” with 您 for an elder (slot change). 近来 is a little formal; in everyday speech 最近 is more usual: 您最近身体怎么样？ means the same (XDHYCD 最近 = the days just before or after now). The 2021 standard has the related “爸爸的身体怎么样？”, and an HSK 2 dialogue “现在身体怎么样？”. The reply you will most likely hear: 还好。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Are you used to it here?
phrases.usage: A question you may hear as a visitor; official 问候 list “对……习惯了吗？” (slot: 这儿, 这儿的天气, 中国菜…). Answers from the same list: 已经习惯了 / 还不太习惯. On a short visit the family is more likely to ask about the food: 中国菜吃得惯吗？ (see that item).
phrases.speaker: them

slots.meaning: what you might not be used to

phrases.regional_note: 这儿 is the erhua (northern) form of 这里 (XDHYCD 这儿 = 这里); in the south you will mostly hear 对这里习惯了吗？

phrases.pinyin_as_source: checker (CC-CEDICT citation tones; 吃得惯 is a potential-complement form, checked word by word)
phrases.english: Are you used to Chinese food? / Is the food OK for you?
phrases.usage: A question you may hear at the table. 吃得惯 = you can eat it without trouble, you are used to it (XDHYCD 吃得来: 吃得惯); the negative 吃不惯 is common in native-written dialogue (“我爸妈吃不惯西餐”, CrossWOZ), and a restaurant helper asks “不知你和朋友是否吃得惯” (RiSAWOZ). Answer 吃得惯 (and praise something: 很好吃！). Slot: the food (中国菜 / 这儿的菜 / 辣的).
phrases.speaker: them

phrases.pinyin: Nǐ yī ge yuè zhuàn duōshao?
phrases.english: How much do you earn a month?
phrases.usage: Adapted from Tatoeba “他一个月赚多少？” (How much does he earn per month?) with the person slot 他 -> 你. Relatives do ask about income at family gatherings (New Year features in Chinese media list it among the awkward questions; a Taiwanese analysis calls it the hardest one — say little and you are looked down on, say a lot and you are showing off). A vague answer such as 还可以 and a change of subject is the usual way out; see the rule on personal questions.
phrases.speaker: them
phrases.regional_note: XDHYCD labels 赚 in the sense “to earn (wages)” as dialectal (〈方〉) and gives 挣钱 as the standard word, so in the north you will often hear 你一个月挣多少？ (zhèng). Both are understood everywhere.

phrases.english: Let's talk about that later.
phrases.usage: Soft way to put off a question or request; listed under 拒绝 (declining) in the official list, and XDHYCD 再说❶ = “表示留待以后办理或考虑” (leave it to be dealt with or considered later). With elders asking about marriage, children or salary, say it lightly and with a smile, or give a vague, friendly answer and change the subject: in a China Youth Daily survey, 59.2% of unmarried young people facing pressure to marry change the subject and 53.0% simply agree with whatever is said. Said flatly, 以后再说吧 can sound as if you are closing the topic.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: You flatter me. / That's too kind.
phrases.usage: Modest answer to a compliment. XDHYCD: 过奖 = 谦辞 “used when the other person praises you”, example “您～了，我不过做了该做的事。”; the official list of modest replies (谦虚) has 过奖了; Tatoeba “过奖了。” = “I'm flattered.” Still common and polite today, especially to elders, and a little formal; native-written dialogue has “谢谢，您过奖了……”. A plain 谢谢 (often with a modest note, e.g. 谢谢，我还在学习) is also fine.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.pinyin_as_source: nǎ•lǐ (XDHYCD headword 哪里); CC-CEDICT na3 li3 na3 li3
phrases.english: Oh, not at all. (deflecting a compliment)
phrases.usage: The textbook modest reply to praise: XDHYCD 哪里❺ “谦辞，用来婉转地推辞对自己的褒奖” with the exchange “你这篇文章写得真好！” — “哪里，哪里！”; in the official 谦虚 list; the keyed answer to “大家都说你是公司里最好的员工” in an official BCT sample; Tatoeba “哪里哪里！”. Today it is still understood everywhere and is fine with elders, but many teachers note that it sounds bookish and old-fashioned; among peers people more often say 没有没有 / 哪有, or simply 谢谢. A natural combination: 哪里哪里，还差得远呢.

phrases.english: Thank you — I'm still learning.
phrases.usage: A natural modern reply when someone says 你中文说得真好: accept with 谢谢 and add a modest note. Teaching sites recommend this middle way rather than a bare 谢谢 or the old-fashioned 哪里哪里; variants they give: 过奖了，我还在学习 / 没有没有，我还需要多练习.

rules.rule: 吃了吗？ (“Have you eaten?”) around mealtimes is a greeting, not an invitation; greeting someone by asking about what they are evidently doing (上课去呀？ “off to class?”, 去哪儿了？ “where have you been?”, 回来啦！ “you're back!”) works the same way. Today it is heard mostly from older people and between neighbours or acquaintances; many younger urban people just say 你好 or “hi”. Answer briefly and return it: 吃了，您呢？ (or 我吃过了。 / 我还没吃。).
rules.why: The official 2002 function list files these under 1. 打招呼 (greeting) with the notes “[吃饭前后]” (before/after meals), “[估计对方作什么就问什么]” (ask about what you guess the other person is doing) and “以下多用于中国人之间” (mostly used between Chinese people). Current usage: Language Log (only between people who know each other; young people may just say hi), The World of Chinese and GoEast Mandarin (typical of the older generation; not an invitation; usual reply 吃了，你呢？), seen as WebSearch summaries.

rules.rule: Use 您 (nín, respectful "you") with your partner's parents, grandparents and other elders; they will usually call you 你.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 您 = "你；你们（含敬意）" (you, with respect), example "老师，～早！"; the polite question "您做什么工作？" is used to an adult in an HSK 2 sample. That elders use 你 to younger people is shown by the sample dialogues (e.g. "你的中文说得不错"), not stated as a rule.
rules.regional_note: 您 is much more frequent in northern (especially Beijing) speech; in the south many people use 你 even with older relatives. Using 您 to your partner's parents is still polite everywhere; if they make it clear that 你 is fine, follow their lead.

rules.rule: Answering a compliment with a modest deflection is still the norm, but the everyday forms have changed: in everyday speech 没有没有 / 哪有 are more common, or people accept with 谢谢 plus a modest note (谢谢，我还在学习). 您过奖了 and 还差得远呢 are polite and common, especially with elders; 哪里哪里 is understood everywhere but sounds bookish and old-fashioned to many younger speakers; 不敢当 is formal.
rules.why: The official 2002 list has a whole function “93. 谦虚” (modesty) with 哪里哪里 / 还差得远呢 / 马马虎虎吧 / 过奖了 / 不敢当; XDHYCD labels 过奖 and 哪里❺ as 谦辞 (humble words) for declining praise; the 2021 grammar standard still teaches 不敢当 (point 309). Current usage: teaching sites (That's Mandarin, DigMandarin, elon.io and others; WebSearch summaries) agree that 哪里哪里 now sounds bookish to many, that 没有没有 is the common colloquial reply, and that 谢谢 with a modest note is a natural middle way; native-written dialogue has 没有没有，您太客气了 and 谢谢，您过奖了 (RiSAWOZ).

rules.rule: 你多大了 is the everyday way to ask someone's age (you will hear it). To ask an older person, the everyday polite form is 您今年多大岁数了？ (XDHYCD 岁数, marked 〈口〉 colloquial: 他今年多大岁数了？); 高寿 is the respectful word for the very old (老大爷高寿啦？), and 贵庚 is a formal honorific for asking anyone's age.
rules.why: XDHYCD: 岁数 〈口〉 “人的年龄：……他今年多大～了？”; 高寿 ❷ “敬辞，用于问老人的年纪”; 贵庚 “敬辞，问人年龄”. 你多大了 is the everyday form (Tatoeba, HSK 1 sample).

rules.rule: Expect personal questions from the elders: your job (你做什么工作？), age (你多大了？), income (你一个月赚多少？) and, above all, marriage and children (你们什么时候结婚？ / 什么时候要孩子？). These questions are common at Chinese family gatherings — Chinese media publish features around Spring Festival on how to handle them. You do not have to answer precisely: a vague, friendly answer and a change of subject is the usual way out (还可以; 以后再说吧 said lightly), and your partner can field the hardest ones.
rules.why: Chinese media features on the questions relatives ask at Spring Festival (China Daily 2016; China News Service 2023/2024) and a Taiwanese analysis of the salary question; China News Service reports a China Youth Daily survey in which 59.2% of unmarried young people facing pressure to marry change the subject and 53.0% simply agree with whatever is said (all seen as WebSearch summaries). The 2025 HSK syllabus lists understanding family members' questions about work as a basic task.

scenes.title: Chinese New Year (春节 / 过年)
scenes.description: Greeting the partner's family over the Spring Festival: wishes for grandparents, children and colleagues, the New Year call (拜年), the reunion dinner and the Gala, zodiac small talk and festival taboos. The 2026 Year of the Horse began on 17 Feb 2026; the next Spring Festival is Sat 6 Feb 2027 (Year of the Goat/Sheep, New Year's Eve Fri 5 Feb 2027).

phrases.pinyin_as_source: guònián hǎo (LTL); 过年 guònián (HSK 2025 level 2)
phrases.english: Happy New Year! (Spring Festival greeting)
phrases.usage: The default spoken greeting for the Spring Festival period, above all when you visit relatives (LTL: “Spring Festival only, especially when visiting relatives”); the new HSK syllabus gives it as the New Year greeting to know at level 2 (“过年说‘过年好’”). Say the person's family title first, then the greeting. Expect the same words back (过年好！) or 新年好！. Do not use it for 1 January — it belongs to the lunar New Year.
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: Used across mainland China. In Cantonese-speaking Guangdong 恭喜发财 is the everyday New Year greeting (LTL).

phrases.english: Happy New Year!
phrases.usage: The all-rounder: it works for 1 January and for the Spring Festival, and it is the usual wording on cards and in WeChat messages (LTL; the HSK 2 syllabus lists “新年快乐” as a greeting-card phrase). phrases.hanzi: 祝您在新的一年身体健康！
phrases.pinyin: Zhù nín zài xīn de yī nián shēntǐ jiànkāng!
phrases.literal: 祝 wish + 您 you (polite) + 在新的一年 in the new year + 身体 body + 健康 healthy
phrases.english: Wishing you good health in the new year!
phrases.usage: A health wish — the standard New Year wish for grandparents, the partner's parents and other elders (use 您; cf. zhihu: children wish elders 身体健康, CCTV: leaders wish elderly people 健康长寿). A shorter form is 祝你身体健康！ (YCT 4, CLEC) — with 您 for elders. In the official YCT sample the speaker adds 幸福快乐！ (answer C = 幸福) and gets the reply 谢谢你！也祝你新春快乐！
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 您 is used far more in northern (especially Beijing) speech; in many southern families 你 is normal even with elders in everyday talk. In a wish to an elder 您 is always polite and never wrong (forum discussions; anecdotal).

phrases.hanzi: 大妈，我们给您拜年来啦！
phrases.pinyin: Dàmā, wǒmen gěi nín bàinián lái la!
phrases.literal: 大妈 auntie + 我们 we + 给您 to you + 拜年 pay a New Year call + 来 come + 啦 (lively particle)
phrases.english: Auntie, we've come to wish you a Happy New Year!
phrases.usage: On the doorstep when you and your partner arrive at a relative's home during the New Year (拜年 = 向人祝贺新年, 现代汉语词典). Replace 大妈 with the person's family title (slot; ask your partner which title each relative gets). Shorter and more formal: 给您拜年了！ — a set New Year-call phrase used mainly on days 1–5 (see rule greeting-timing). Expect 过年好！ in return.
phrases.speaker: me

slots.meaning: the relative you are visiting, by family title (大妈 = the wife of the father's elder brother, i.e. 伯母; also a respectful word for any older woman — 现代汉语词典)

phrases.regional_note: Kinship titles vary by region and family (e.g. 外婆/外公 in most of the south vs 姥姥/姥爷 in the north for the mother's parents); use the titles your partner uses.

phrases.literal: 拜 pay respects + 年 (New) Year
phrases.english: to pay a New Year call; to wish someone a happy New Year
phrases.usage: To congratulate people on the New Year (现代汉语词典: 向人祝贺新年), in person, by phone or by message. The person comes after 给: 给奶奶拜年, 给大家拜年 (CCTV 2023, 2025). Lu Xun's essay 《过年》 already lists it with 放鞭炮 and 恭喜发财. HSK level 6 word (2025 syllabus).

sources.evidence: Search summary (same article on yn.people.com.cn in traditional characters and travel.gmw.cn 2021-02-19; plus Baidu Baike 拜早年 and 《人文松江大辞典》 via The Paper): after the 5th day formal New Year calls stop and people say “拜个晚年”; Peking University folklorist 陈连山: the closest people are visited in the first three days, more distant ones later; quote: “初七，開工！相信回到工作單位上的你一定聽到有同事說‘給您拜個晚年’”; distant relatives can be visited after the Lantern Festival — “称‘拜个晚年’”; “拜早年” from 小年 (north 腊月二十三, south 腊月二十四) until New Year’s Eve (陈连山 via Baidu Baike); proverb “有心拜年，十五不晚”; a local custom note contrasts city people’s “‘拜個早年’‘提前給您拜年了’”. The summary describes 给您拜年了 as the formal New Year-call phrase used mainly from the 1st to the 5th day.

phrases.pinyin_as_source: gōngxǐ fācái (LTL); gōng xǐ fā cái (ChinesePod)
phrases.literal: 恭喜 congratulations + 发财 get rich
phrases.english: Wishing you prosperity! (Kung Hei Fat Choi)
phrases.usage: Wish for wealth in the new year, used all over China and the general New Year greeting in Cantonese-speaking areas (LTL). Natural with colleagues, shopkeepers, friends and family; children cheekily add 红包拿来 (see red-envelope scene). Children bowing to elders combine it with health: 祝您新年快乐，恭喜发财，身体健康 (zhihu).
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: Default New Year greeting in Cantonese-speaking Guangdong; in Beijing and the north 新年好 is more common (LTL).

sources.title: Happy New Year in Chinese: 新年快乐 and Better Ways to Say It
sources.publisher: LTL Mandarin School
sources.evidence: Search summary (search restricted to ltl-school.com; results incl. this page, /chinese-new-year-vocab/, /red-envelope/): 新年快乐 (xīnnián kuàilè) “the standard way, which works on January 1st and at Chinese New Year”, the usual choice for cards and messages; 新年好 (xīnnián hǎo) “Spoken and casual, when you bump into neighbours, friends or colleagues over the holiday”; “In Beijing and northern cities, 新年好 (Xīn Nián Hǎo) is more common than 恭喜发财”; 过年好 (guònián hǎo) “Spring Festival only, especially when visiting relatives”; 春节快乐 (chūnjié kuàilè): “the phrase chūnjié kuàilè would only be used for Chinese New Year or Spring Festival, rather than during Western New Year”; 恭喜发财 (gōngxǐ fācái): “in the South of China, Cantonese-speaking regions in particular, it is used as a general greeting for Chinese New Year” (hence “Kung Hei Fat Choi”); “Children will often follow up 恭喜发财 with the phrase 红包拿来 (hóngbāo ná lái)”; 万事如意 (wànshì rúyì) general-purpose; “Common ones for families and business include 阖家幸福 (family happiness) and 生意兴隆”; 年年有余 (niánnián yǒu yú): “The word 余 sounds like 鱼 (fish), which is why fish is a common New Year dish”; for elders, teachers or clients “one source suggests swapping 你 for the more polite 您 (nín), as in 祝您新年快乐”. The summary did not say which LTL page each line came from.

sources.evidence: Search summary (search restricted to ltl-school.com; results incl. this page, /chinese-new-year-vocab/, /red-envelope/): 新年快乐 (xīnnián kuàilè) “the standard way, which works on January 1st and at Chinese New Year”, the usual choice for cards and messages; 新年好 (xīnnián hǎo) “Spoken and casual, when you bump into neighbours, friends or colleagues over the holiday”; “In Beijing and northern cities, 新年好 (Xīn Nián Hǎo) is more common than 恭喜发财”; 过年好 (guònián hǎo) “Spring Festival only, especially when visiting relatives”; 春节快乐 (chūnjié kuàilè): “the phrase chūnjié kuàilè would only be used for Chinese New Year or Spring Festival, rather than during Western New Year”; 恭喜发财 (gōngxǐ fācái): “in the South of China, Cantonese-speaking regions in particular, it is used as a general greeting for Chinese New Year” (hence “Kung Hei Fat Choi”); “Children will often follow up 恭喜发财 with the phrase 红包拿来 (hóngbāo ná lái)”; 万事如意 (wànshì rúyì) general-purpose; “Common ones for families and business include 阖家幸福 (family happiness) and 生意兴隆”; 年年有余 (niánnián yǒu yú): “The word 余 sounds like 鱼 (fish), which is why fish is a common New Year dish”; for elders, teachers or clients “one source suggests swapping 你 for the more polite 您 (nín), as in 祝您新年快乐”. The summary did not say which LTL page each line came from.

phrases.literal: 三阳 three yang (lines) + 开泰 open into peace and prosperity
phrases.english: May the new year bring good fortune! (classic Goat-year wish)
phrases.usage: Traditional New Year blessing from the Book of Changes (常用以称颂岁首或寓意吉祥, Xinhua idiom data). Because 羊 (goat) sounds like 阳, LTL calls it “the classic Goat-year wish” — so it suits the 2027 Spring Festival; the pun is old (西游记: 设此三羊，以应开泰之言). Literary: use it in a toast, a card or a WeChat message; in conversation 新年快乐 is enough.

phrases.english: I was born in the Year of the Horse.
phrases.usage: Answer to 你属什么？ with your own animal (slot). phrases.literal: 岁岁 year after year (sounds like 碎碎 “broken to pieces”) + 平安 safe and well
phrases.english: Peace year after year! (said at once when something breaks)
phrases.usage: A New Year greeting in its own right (CC-CEDICT), and THE thing to say at once if someone breaks a bowl or a glass during the New Year: 碎 “broken” sounds exactly like 岁 “year”, so the bad omen becomes a wish — The Paper writes it “岁（碎）岁平安” to show the pun. Another saying for the same moment: 落地开花，富贵荣华. When the pun is meant you may also see it written 碎碎平安 (as in the rule taboos).
phrases.speaker: either

sources.title: 大年初一，这些的习俗和禁忌你知道吗？
sources.publisher: 澎湃新闻 The Paper
sources.evidence: Search summary (results: thepaper.cn customs articles, Baidu Baike 农历过年期间禁忌 and 讨吉利, gmw.cn 2022-02-05 “正月初五 ‘破五’ ‘送穷’”): on the 1st day no sweeping or taking out rubbish (the broom’s birthday; sweeping sweeps away luck; if you must, sweep from the door inwards); breaking something is a bad omen and you quickly say “岁（碎）岁平安” or “落地开花，富贵荣华”; avoid words such as 死, 破, 坏 and use 福, 寿, 喜 (Baidu Baike 讨吉利); do not call people by name to get them up on the morning of the 1st; some places avoid knives, scissors and needles on the 1st; the taboos end on the 5th day (破五), when people clean and set off firecrackers; practice varies a lot by place and is simpler today.

phrases.literal: 年年 every year + 有 have + 余 surplus (sounds like 鱼 fish)
phrases.english: May you have abundance year after year
phrases.usage: Auspicious New Year saying (CC-CEDICT) behind the New Year fish: 余 “surplus” sounds like 鱼 “fish”, which is why fish is a common New Year dish (LTL); you will see it on decorations and fish lanterns (CCTV). Many families make sure some of the fish is left over, so that there is “surplus” (余): news features describe not finishing the fish (a custom given for north of the Yangtze), keeping the head and tail until New Year's Day, and in Hubei a “look-at fish” (看鱼) that is served but not eaten. Customs vary — watch what the family does before you finish the fish.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.literal: 放 set off + 鞭炮 (strings of) firecrackers
phrases.english: to set off firecrackers
phrases.usage: Firecrackers belong to festive occasions (现代汉语词典 爆竹: 多用于喜庆事; 放 ❼ 点燃：～爆竹) and above all to the New Year — Lu Xun's essay 《过年》 lists 放鞭炮，打麻将，拜年，“恭喜发财”！. Today many cities ban or restrict them by district, time and type: check the local notice before you join in (see rule firecrackers).
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: Rules differ by city and even district (see rule firecrackers).

rules.rule: Spring Festival dates: 2026 was the Year of the Horse (丙午马年): New Year's Eve (除夕) Mon 16 Feb 2026, Spring Festival (正月初一) Tue 17 Feb 2026, public holiday 15–23 Feb (9 days; make-up workdays Sat 14 Feb and Sat 28 Feb). Next: Year of the Goat/Sheep (丁未羊年) — New Year's Eve Fri 5 Feb 2027, Spring Festival Sat 6 Feb 2027, Lantern Festival Sat 20 Feb 2027. By law the Spring Festival holiday is 4 statutory days (除夕 to 初三), stretched by weekend swaps; the official 2027 arrangement had not been published on 2026-11-02 (the 2026 one was published in November 2025).
rules.why: Travel to the family has to be booked around these dates; greetings switch from “early” to “happy” to “late” New Year around them.

rules.rule: Timing of New Year wishes: from 小年 (23rd day of the 12th lunar month in the north, 24th in the south) until New Year's Eve you wish people an early New Year (拜个早年); from New Year's Day you say 过年好/新年好/新年快乐 and pay New Year calls (拜年) — closest family first, mainly days 1–5; after that, or when you first meet after the holiday, wishes become “late” (拜个晚年), and the New Year season in the broad sense lasts until the Lantern Festival (正月十五): 有心拜年，十五不晚. In 2027: 小年 Sat 30 Jan (north) / Sun 31 Jan (south); New Year's Eve Fri 5 Feb.
rules.why: Matching the wish to the date is part of sounding natural; a late wish is still welcome.
rules.regional_note: 小年 falls on 腊月二十三 in the north and 腊月二十四 in the south (陈连山 via Baidu Baike, People's Daily 2021); exact visiting customs vary by family and region.

sources.title: 用这些拜年小知识，给您“拜个晚年”
sources.publisher: 人民网 People’s Daily Online (陕西频道)
sources.evidence: Search summary (same article on yn.people.com.cn in traditional characters and travel.gmw.cn 2021-02-19; plus Baidu Baike 拜早年 and 《人文松江大辞典》 via The Paper): after the 5th day formal New Year calls stop and people say “拜个晚年”; Peking University folklorist 陈连山: the closest people are visited in the first three days, more distant ones later; quote: “初七，開工！相信回到工作單位上的你一定聽到有同事說‘給您拜個晚年’”; distant relatives can be visited after the Lantern Festival — “称‘拜个晚年’”; “拜早年” from 小年 (north 腊月二十三, south 腊月二十四) until New Year’s Eve (陈连山 via Baidu Baike); proverb “有心拜年，十五不晚”; a local custom note contrasts city people’s “‘拜個早年’‘提前給您拜年了’”. The summary describes 给您拜年了 as the formal New Year-call phrase used mainly from the 1st to the 5th day.

rules.rule: Choose the wish for the person: elders (grandparents, the partner's parents) — use 您 and wish health and long life (身体健康, 健康长寿, 万事如意); school-age children and students — 学业进步 (or 学习进步, 快快长大 for small children); working adults and colleagues — 工作顺利, 步步高升, 恭喜发财; anyone — 新年快乐, 过年好, 万事如意, 心想事成 (friends, students). Several wishes are often chained: 身体健康、工作顺利、阖家幸福.
rules.why: Wishes are matched to the person's stage of life (LTL/search summary: students → 学业进步, anyone → 万事如意; CCTV: elderly people → 健康长寿).
rules.regional_note: 您 is used far more in northern (especially Beijing) speech; in many southern families 你 is normal even with elders in everyday talk. In a wish to an elder 您 is always polite and never wrong (forum discussions; anecdotal).

sources.title: Happy New Year in Chinese: 新年快乐 and Better Ways to Say It (multi-site search)
sources.publisher: LTL Mandarin School (most likely page; see evidence)
sources.evidence: Multi-site search summary (results: 4 ltl-school.com pages, 4 chinesepod.com pages, goeastmandarin.com “Chinese Greetings for Chinese New Year”, 2 yoyochinese.com posts); lines were not attributed to a page, but the table wording matches the LTL article: “新年快乐 | xīnnián kuàilè | Happy New Year | The all-rounder: cards, WeChat messages, January 1st and Chinese New Year”; 万事如意 (wànshì rúyì) “suitable for anyone”; 心想事成 (xīn xiǎng shì chéng) “suited to friends and students”; 学业进步 (xuéyè jìnbù) “Progress in your studies,” for students; a longer wish 恭贺新禧，祝身体健康、事业发达; “Use 您 (nín) instead of 你 (nǐ) with elders, teachers, or clients. For grandparents, teachers, your boss or a client, swap 你 for the polite 您 (nín).”; “Many longer wishes begin with 祝你 (zhù nǐ)”. 工作顺利 did not appear in these results.

sources.title: Happy New Year in Chinese: 新年快乐 and Better Ways to Say It
sources.publisher: LTL Mandarin School
sources.evidence: Search summary (search restricted to ltl-school.com; results incl. this page, /chinese-new-year-vocab/, /red-envelope/): 新年快乐 (xīnnián kuàilè) “the standard way, which works on January 1st and at Chinese New Year”, the usual choice for cards and messages; 新年好 (xīnnián hǎo) “Spoken and casual, when you bump into neighbours, friends or colleagues over the holiday”; “In Beijing and northern cities, 新年好 (Xīn Nián Hǎo) is more common than 恭喜发财”; 过年好 (guònián hǎo) “Spring Festival only, especially when visiting relatives”; 春节快乐 (chūnjié kuàilè): “the phrase chūnjié kuàilè would only be used for Chinese New Year or Spring Festival, rather than during Western New Year”; 恭喜发财 (gōngxǐ fācái): “in the South of China, Cantonese-speaking regions in particular, it is used as a general greeting for Chinese New Year” (hence “Kung Hei Fat Choi”); “Children will often follow up 恭喜发财 with the phrase 红包拿来 (hóngbāo ná lái)”; 万事如意 (wànshì rúyì) general-purpose; “Common ones for families and business include 阖家幸福 (family happiness) and 生意兴隆”; 年年有余 (niánnián yǒu yú): “The word 余 sounds like 鱼 (fish), which is why fish is a common New Year dish”; for elders, teachers or clients “one source suggests swapping 你 for the more polite 您 (nín), as in 祝您新年快乐”. rules.rule: Festival taboos (strongest on the 1st day, lifted on the 5th, 破五): avoid unlucky words such as 死 (death), 破 (broken), 坏 (bad) and prefer lucky ones (福, 寿, 喜); many families do not sweep or take out rubbish on the 1st day (it “sweeps away” luck — if you must, sweep inwards); if something breaks, say 碎碎平安 (or 落地开花，富贵荣华); some places avoid knives, scissors and needles on the 1st day and avoid calling people by name to wake them on New Year's morning.
rules.why: These are folk beliefs that many families still keep in a simplified form; following the family's lead avoids awkward moments.
rules.regional_note: Practice varies a lot between regions and families and is simpler today (The Paper / Baidu Baike); ask your partner which ones the family keeps.

rules.rule: Firecrackers and fireworks are regulated city by city: under the State Council's 烟花爆竹安全管理条例 (art. 28) county-level and higher governments may restrict or ban them by time, place and type, and art. 30 bans them near cultural relics, stations and airports, etc. For the 2026 Spring Festival e.g. Nanjing kept bans in its central districts, Taiyuan banned them in all six urban districts, Zhengzhou banned them inside the 4th Ring Road but allowed them outside in set hours (e.g. New Year's Eve 07:00 to 01:00), and Yuncheng changed a full ban into restrictions; many places allow private use of small C/D-class products only. Check the local notice (通告) each year before setting any off; in April 2026 the State Council safety office started a one-year national crackdown on illegal fireworks.
rules.why: Setting off fireworks at a banned time or place is fined 100–500 yuan by the police (art. 42); the rules change from year to year and district to district.
rules.regional_note: Varies by city and even district; in 2026 outer districts were often more permissive than city centres (e.g. Zhengzhou outside the 4th Ring Road, Nanjing's central-district bans).

rules.rule: New Year's Eve is for the family reunion dinner (年夜饭/团圆饭) and the CCTV Gala, followed by staying up (守岁, 现代汉语词典: 在农历除夕晚上不睡觉，直到天亮). Dumplings are a must on New Year's Eve in northern China; southern tables have other symbolic foods — 年糕 (“higher year”; 现代汉语词典: 农历年的应时食品), fish and regional dishes, and in some southern areas sweet rice balls (汤圆) on the morning of New Year's Day. Fish is served for 年年有余 because 鱼 sounds like 余, and many families leave some of it uneaten — or keep the head and tail until New Year's Day — so that there is “surplus”; in Hubei a “look-at fish” (看鱼) is not eaten at all.
rules.why: Knowing the symbolism lets you comment on the dishes appropriately; do not assume a southern family will make dumplings.
rules.regional_note: Dumplings are a northern tradition; the partner's south/central family may serve 年糕, fish or regional dishes (e.g. CCTV 2023: families in Longyan, Fujian preparing 腊肉、笋干、手打牛肉丸 for the reunion dinner). Fish customs vary (not finished north of the Yangtze; head and tail kept for New Year's Day elsewhere; 看鱼 in Hubei) — watch the family before finishing the fish.

rules.rule: New Year visits follow an order: the 1st day is spent with the (husband's) family; in many regions married daughters return to their parents' home on the 2nd day (回娘家) with husband and children, bringing gifts in even numbers, and a son-in-law pays his respects to his wife's parents. The day differs locally (e.g. Qingdao on the 3rd, Dezhou on the 4th day).
rules.why: If you are married into the family, which day you visit whose parents is a real planning question — ask your partner what their family does.
rules.regional_note: Widespread on the 2nd day — e.g. Shandong, Hebei, Guangdong (Chaoshan and Hakka families), northern and central Shanxi, Henan (which also has a visit on the 16th of the 1st month) — but the day differs locally: Qingdao on the 3rd, Dezhou on the 4th, southern Shanxi mostly on the 3rd. Ask your partner's family.

rules.rule: The zodiac animal changes at the lunar New Year, not on 1 January: 2026 = Horse (马, 丙午), 2027 = Goat/Sheep (羊, 丁未; from 6 Feb 2027 to 25 Jan 2028). 羊 covers goat, sheep and ram in English. Your own animal's year (本命年) comes every 12 years. You may hear the folk saying 十羊九不全 about Goat-year people — it is folklore (LTL).
rules.why: Zodiac questions and wishes are standard New Year small talk.

phrases.literal: 谢谢 thank you + 奶奶 Grandma (father's mother)
phrases.english: Thank you, Grandma!
phrases.usage: As you take a red envelope: both hands, thanks with the giver's family title, then a New Year wish; put it away unopened and open it later at home (zhihu; LTL). Slot change: the official YCT model is 谢谢王老师 (“thank you, Teacher Wang”); we put a family title in the slot. Ask your partner which title each relative gets (see the family-address-kinship topic).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 奶奶/爷爷 = the father's parents. For the mother's parents relationship.js lists 外婆 first in its main data and switches to 姥姥 (姥爷) only in its northern locale; 现代汉语词典 has 姥姥 unmarked and 外婆/外公 marked 〈方〉 (regional). So 姥姥/姥爷 is the northern form and 外婆/外公 the default elsewhere — use what the partner's family uses (see the family-address-kinship topic).

sources.title: 当亲戚赠与我们红包时，我们为什么要在表面上过分推辞？我们该不该这么做？ - 知乎
sources.publisher: 知乎 Zhihu (community Q&A)
sources.evidence: Search summary of this and related posts (zhihu.com/question/513979659 “怎样教孩子收红包礼仪？”, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/602649524, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/20161267814): refusing has no fixed pattern and can be skipped — “若收红包，请双手接，给长辈敬个礼。并说‘谢谢’”; if you will accept anyway, ritual refusal is unnecessary, accept calmly and say thanks; refusing is more common with relatives you are not close to, as a show of politeness; a suggested blessing when receiving: bow and say “祝您新年快乐，恭喜发财，身体健康”; take the envelope with both hands; never open it in front of the giver (look at home); do not announce the amount. No source gave a fixed number of refusals.

phrases.pinyin: Zhù nín xīnnián kuàilè, shēntǐ jiànkāng!
phrases.pinyin_as_source: Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè, shēntǐ jiànkāng (ChinesePod, with 你)
phrases.literal: 祝 wish + 您 you (polite) + 新年快乐 happy New Year + 身体健康 good health
phrases.english: Happy New Year and good health to you!

sources.title: Chinese New Year Red Envelopes: How to Give and Receive “hóngbāo” Like a Local
sources.publisher: ChinesePod
sources.evidence: Search summary (teaching sites incl. this page and thechairmansbao.com “Why Do Chinese People Give Red Envelopes?”): recipients are expected to recite a New Year blessing before accepting; one source gives “Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè, shēntǐ jiànkāng” as a common example; another says to thank the giver, extend a greeting and open the envelope only once you are home; crisp new bills, no coins; 恭喜发财，红包拿来！ is a playful line, “a joke rather than a polite phrase”.

sources.title: 当亲戚赠与我们红包时，我们为什么要在表面上过分推辞？我们该不该这么做？ - 知乎
sources.publisher: 知乎 Zhihu (community Q&A)
sources.evidence: Search summary of this and related posts (zhihu.com/question/513979659 “怎样教孩子收红包礼仪？”, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/602649524, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/20161267814): refusing has no fixed pattern and can be skipped — “若收红包，请双手接，给长辈敬个礼。并说‘谢谢’”; if you will accept anyway, ritual refusal is unnecessary, accept calmly and say thanks; refusing is more common with relatives you are not close to, as a show of politeness; a suggested blessing when receiving: bow and say “祝您新年快乐，恭喜发财，身体健康”; take the envelope with both hands; never open it in front of the giver (look at home); do not announce the amount. No source gave a fixed number of refusals.

sources.title: Happy New Year in Chinese: 新年快乐 and Better Ways to Say It
sources.publisher: LTL Mandarin School
sources.evidence: Search summary (search restricted to ltl-school.com; results incl. this page, /chinese-new-year-vocab/, /red-envelope/): 新年快乐 (xīnnián kuàilè) “the standard way, which works on January 1st and at Chinese New Year”, the usual choice for cards and messages; 新年好 (xīnnián hǎo) “Spoken and casual, when you bump into neighbours, friends or colleagues over the holiday”; “In Beijing and northern cities, 新年好 (Xīn Nián Hǎo) is more common than 恭喜发财”; 过年好 (guònián hǎo) “Spring Festival only, especially when visiting relatives”; 春节快乐 (chūnjié kuàilè): “the phrase chūnjié kuàilè would only be used for Chinese New Year or Spring Festival, rather than during Western New Year”; 恭喜发财 (gōngxǐ fācái): “in the South of China, Cantonese-speaking regions in particular, it is used as a general greeting for Chinese New Year” (hence “Kung Hei Fat Choi”); “Children will often follow up 恭喜发财 with the phrase 红包拿来 (hóngbāo ná lái)”; 万事如意 (wànshì rúyì) general-purpose; “Common ones for families and business include 阖家幸福 (family happiness) and 生意兴隆”; 年年有余 (niánnián yǒu yú): “The word 余 sounds like 鱼 (fish), which is why fish is a common New Year dish”; for elders, teachers or clients “one source suggests swapping 你 for the more polite 您 (nín), as in 祝您新年快乐”. The summary did not say which LTL page each line came from.

sources.title: Giving Red Envelopes · Chinese Lesson
sources.publisher: ChinesePod
sources.evidence: Search summary: “For Chinese New Year, it’s customary for older members of the family to give red envelopes filled with money (红包, hóngbāo) to the younger members of the family.” The dialogue is about a newly married woman who learns she now has to give them too. The related dictionary entry for 压岁钱 says 红包, 红包袋 and 压岁钱 are used interchangeably.

sources.title: Red Envelope (Hóng Bāo 红包) 🧧 FAQ’s Answered (+ Facts & Figures)
sources.publisher: LTL Mandarin School
sources.evidence: Search summary (restricted to ltl-school.com; this page = result 1): the giver is usually “an older relative, family friend, or neighbor”, married couples may also give to single people; another line advises giving only to people younger than you; once you start earning, custom expects you to give to your parents and grandparents; avoid the number 4 (sounds like “death”); multiples of 8 such as 80 or 800 are lucky; crisp new banknotes are preferred, worn notes are poor form; accept the envelope with both hands and do not open it right away or in front of the giver; digital hongbao are a common way to send greetings to friends and coworkers.

sources.title: 男朋友第一次来女方家，要给女方家所有的亲人包红包吗? - 知乎
sources.publisher: 知乎 Zhihu (community Q&A)
sources.evidence: Search summary of this and related questions (zhihu.com/question/442420115 “第一次跟男朋友（广东人）去他家见爸妈，但是没收到红包是什么意思？”, zhihu.com/question/67478834 “带女朋友第一次正式见我父母，应该给多少红包？”, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/19321479715): no fixed rule, it depends on local custom; “长辈给晚辈、已婚给未婚发红包，所以未婚男友不一定需要给长辈发红包”, “一般是过年时长辈包给小孩，已婚给未婚，领导给下属”; some places expect a return gift on the first visit and gifts for the family are appropriate; for close grandparents “他们并不在乎红包金额的大小”, 100–500 yuan with a written blessing is a common range, or gifts (烟酒、水果) plus a red envelope; if the girlfriend has under-age younger siblings, give each one an envelope, “数目是百的偶数就可以了”; another article: 50–200 yuan is a common range for minors; give several children the same amount; avoid 4 and 250; safest is to ask the partner about the family’s custom.

sources.title: 当亲戚赠与我们红包时，我们为什么要在表面上过分推辞？我们该不该这么做？ - 知乎
sources.publisher: 知乎 Zhihu (community Q&A)
sources.evidence: Search summary of this and related posts (zhihu.com/question/513979659 “怎样教孩子收红包礼仪？”, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/602649524, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/20161267814): refusing has no fixed pattern and can be skipped — “若收红包，请双手接，给长辈敬个礼。并说‘谢谢’”; if you will accept anyway, ritual refusal is unnecessary, accept calmly and say thanks; refusing is more common with relatives you are not close to, as a show of politeness; a suggested blessing when receiving: bow and say “祝您新年快乐，恭喜发财，身体健康”; take the envelope with both hands; never open it in front of the giver (look at home); do not announce the amount. No source gave a fixed number of refusals.

phrases.literal: 抢 grab + 红包 red packet
phrases.english: to grab (WeChat) red packets
phrases.usage: In WeChat groups a red packet is split into shares and whoever taps first gets one, so families and colleagues “grab” them — especially on New Year's Eve. The amount of each share is decided at random by WeChat's server (The Paper).
phrases.speaker: either

sources.title: 抢微信红包有没有“最佳手气”攻略？红包上限为什么是200元？微信回应
sources.publisher: 澎湃新闻 The Paper
sources.evidence: Search summary (also thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_32625313 “第二个抢微信红包最容易手气最佳？微信官方回应”): WeChat says the amount of each share is randomly assigned by the server when the packet is created, so “手气最佳” (best luck) tips have no basis; people prefer the luck-based (手气) red packet to the ordinary one with equal shares; the headline refers to a 200-yuan upper limit per red packet. “Whoever gets 手气最佳 sends the next one” is a group game, not a universal rule (summary of zhihu “微信群红包的47种玩法”); a school study is summarised as “抢红包人数会影响‘手气王’概率吗？”. No source for a “谢谢老板” etiquette rule was found.

phrases.literal: 不用 no need + 了 (change of situation) + 谢谢 thanks
phrases.english: No, thank you.
phrases.usage: A polite “no, thanks”. With red envelopes a token refusal is optional: zhihu answers say it is more common with relatives you are not close to, and from close elders you simply accept with both hands and thanks — there is no fixed number of refusals. If you do refuse once, accept when they insist.

sources.title: 当亲戚赠与我们红包时，我们为什么要在表面上过分推辞？我们该不该这么做？ - 知乎
sources.publisher: 知乎 Zhihu (community Q&A)
sources.evidence: Search summary of this and related posts (zhihu.com/question/513979659 “怎样教孩子收红包礼仪？”, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/602649524, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/20161267814): refusing has no fixed pattern and can be skipped — “若收红包，请双手接，给长辈敬个礼。并说‘谢谢’”; if you will accept anyway, ritual refusal is unnecessary, accept calmly and say thanks; refusing is more common with relatives you are not close to, as a show of politeness; a suggested blessing when receiving: bow and say “祝您新年快乐，恭喜发财，身体健康”; take the envelope with both hands; never open it in front of the giver (look at home); do not announce the amount. No source gave a fixed number of refusals.

phrases.english: first-meeting gift
phrases.usage: A gift at a first meeting, usually from the older to the younger (现代汉语词典: 多指年长对年幼的). When a partner is brought home to meet the parents, the parents often give them a red envelope: zhihu threads ask how much to give the girlfriend at the first formal meeting, and what it means if a Guangdong boyfriend's parents gave none. Accept it with both hands and thanks.

sources.title: 男朋友第一次来女方家，要给女方家所有的亲人包红包吗? - 知乎
sources.publisher: 知乎 Zhihu (community Q&A)
sources.evidence: Search summary of this and related questions (zhihu.com/question/442420115 “第一次跟男朋友（广东人）去他家见爸妈，但是没收到红包是什么意思？”, zhihu.com/question/67478834 “带女朋友第一次正式见我父母，应该给多少红包？”, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/19321479715): no fixed rule, it depends on local custom; “长辈给晚辈、已婚给未婚发红包，所以未婚男友不一定需要给长辈发红包”, “一般是过年时长辈包给小孩，已婚给未婚，领导给下属”; some places expect a return gift on the first visit and gifts for the family are appropriate; for close grandparents “他们并不在乎红包金额的大小”, 100–500 yuan with a written blessing is a common range, or gifts (烟酒、水果) plus a red envelope; if the girlfriend has under-age younger siblings, give each one an envelope, “数目是百的偶数就可以了”; another article: 50–200 yuan is a common range for minors; give several children the same amount; avoid 4 and 250; safest is to ask the partner about the family’s custom.

rules.rule: Red envelopes go from older to younger and from married to unmarried: grandparents, parents, aunts and uncles give to children and to unmarried young adults (bosses also give to staff). Once you earn money you are expected to give to your own parents and grandparents, and once you marry you become a giver to the family's children.
rules.why: The envelope expresses the elder's care and good wishes (CCTV: 长辈对他们的关爱与期望); marriage moves you from the receiving to the giving side.

sources.title: Red Envelope (Hóng Bāo 红包) 🧧 FAQ’s Answered (+ Facts & Figures)
sources.publisher: LTL Mandarin School
sources.evidence: Search summary (restricted to ltl-school.com; this page = result 1): the giver is usually “an older relative, family friend, or neighbor”, married couples may also give to single people; another line advises giving only to people younger than you; once you start earning, custom expects you to give to your parents and grandparents; avoid the number 4 (sounds like “death”); multiples of 8 such as 80 or 800 are lucky; crisp new banknotes are preferred, worn notes are poor form; accept the envelope with both hands and do not open it right away or in front of the giver; digital hongbao are a common way to send greetings to friends and coworkers.

sources.title: 男朋友第一次来女方家，要给女方家所有的亲人包红包吗? - 知乎

sources.evidence: Search summary of this and related questions (zhihu.com/question/442420115 “第一次跟男朋友（广东人）去他家见爸妈，但是没收到红包是什么意思？”, zhihu.com/question/67478834 “带女朋友第一次正式见我父母，应该给多少红包？”, zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/19321479715): no fixed rule, it depends on local custom; “长辈给晚辈、已婚给未婚发红包，所以未婚男友不一定需要给长辈发红包”, “一般是过年时长辈包给小孩，已婚给未婚，领导给下属”; some places expect a return gift on the first visit and gifts for the family are appropriate; for close grandparents “他们并不在乎红包金额的大小”, 100–500 yuan with a written blessing is a common range, or gifts (烟酒、水果) plus a red envelope; if the girlfriend has under-age younger siblings, give each one an envelope, “数目是百的偶数就可以了”; another article: 50–200 yuan is a common range for minors; give several children the same amount; avoid 4 and 250; safest is to ask the partner about the family’s custom.
